Article Title: OpenAI expands GPT-6 lineup with cheaper, faster Sol and Luna models
Article Text:
Cheaper models built on the same foundation

How the new models perform

Key features

Availability

OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims that Sol is designed as a high-performance model optimised for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. On the other hand, Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases and offer faster responses and lower compute requirements. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques, including safeguards around recursive self-improvement (RSI) and improved oversight mechanisms. OpenAI also stressed on the fact that the launch reflects its commitment to balancing innovation with safety, ensuring that frontier AI systems remain under human control while scaling their capabilities.Earlier this month, OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as the most intelligent and aligned model it has built to date. Sol and Luna extend that same generation of intelligence downward, trained using similar methods as Astra but optimized to advance the frontier on cost efficiency rather than raw capability. OpenAI says the two new models bring Astra's advances in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable tiers.The economics are the headline change here. Thanks to improvements in caching and inference, OpenAI is cutting API prices for both models by 50% compared to their GPT-5.6 promotional pricing. GPT-6 Sol now costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down from $4 and $20 respectively. GPT-6 Luna is even cheaper, dropping to $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20. Astra remains OpenAI's top recommendation when uncompromising performance matters most.OpenAI is positioning Sol in particular as a serious contender against rival models at a fraction of the cost. On AutomationBench, a test of real-world business workflows, the company says GPT-6 Sol at its highest effort setting outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 at max effort while costing just 9% as much per task. On Agents' Last Exam, which evaluates complex, long-horizon professional workflows, Sol scored 56.4% at max effort — ahead of Opus 5's best score in the same evaluation, at 60% lower cost per task.Coding performance also saw a notable jump. On FrontierCode, which grades AI-generated code on whether it's actually ready to merge into real codebases, OpenAI says Sol improved substantially over its GPT-5.6 predecessor and now matches Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 at a much lower price. On a separate software-engineering benchmark, DeepSWE, Sol scored within roughly one percentage point of Fable 5's best result while costing about 80% less per task.Factuality — long a weak point for large language models — also improved meaningfully. Based on OpenAI's internal evaluation using real conversations where users had previously flagged mistakes, Sol now makes roughly half as many factual errors as its predecessor, approaching Astra-level reliability at a fraction of the cost.* Sol: Advanced reasoning, multi‑step task automation, and integration with scientific and enterprise workflows.* Luna: Lightweight deployment, optimized for consumer applications, and faster performance on smaller devices.* Shared Advances: Improved multilingual support, adaptive memory, and enhanced contextual understanding across domains.GPT-6 Sol and Luna are rolling out today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Free and Go users can access Luna through the desktop app. Neither model is yet available in standard Chat. Developers can access both through the OpenAI API as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna. OpenAI said the rollout within ChatGPT will happen gradually throughout the day to keep the service stable.
Article Summary: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. GPT-6 Sol is designed for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques.

Article Title: Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 is faster, cheaper and matches Fable 5.1 on most work
Article Text:
Anthropic's new Claude Opus 5.5 is 40% cheaper than Opus 5

Claude Opus 5.5 pricing undercuts Opus 5 on every token

Opus 5.5 leads benchmarks in coding and knowledge work

Anthropic adds Fable-level safeguards for biology and cybersecurity

Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessor.This is Anthropic's first release since it called for pacing the AI frontier, so safety features sit right next to performance. Opus 5.5 was tested before launch by external evaluators, including METR and Frontier Design. Anthropic says it scored the best of any model on its automated behavioural audit, which runs nearly 2,000 simulated scenarios. The model is available now on the Claude Platform as claude-opus-5-5, and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.Input tokens cost $4 (about Rs 350) per million and output tokens $20 (about Rs 1,760), both 20% lower than Opus 5. Cache reads, which Anthropic says make up most of the bill in agentic and coding work, drop 60% to $0.20 (about Rs 18) per million. Opus 5.5 also uses fewer tokens per task, which is where the overall 40% saving comes from.Subscribers benefit too. Anthropic is raising five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans. Users also get a rate limit reset they can save and use whenever they choose.On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Opus 5.5 scored 66.4%, ahead of Fable 5.1 at 55.8% and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 57.9%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, which tests real-world work across 44 occupations, it posted 1846 Elo against 1708 for Opus 5.Anthropic also shared results from actual workloads. One early tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in under a day. In an internal test, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both rewrote HAProxy, a widely used load balancer, from C into Rust. Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours against 12 and cost 51% less.The company says the model writes more clearly as well. It puts key information first and avoids jargon, which responds to a common complaint about Opus 5.Opus 5.5 matches Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so it ships with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. Developers can still find and fix bugs in their own code, but most cybersecurity tasks will be rerouted to Opus 4.8. Vetted labs, startups and pharmaceutical firms can apply to a new Life Sciences Verification Program. Verified security practitioners will get access through an expanded Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks.Anthropic acknowledges some limits. It says Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which makes its real-world behaviour harder to predict. The company is pairing its alignment work with these safeguards for that reason.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 are due in the coming weeks. For now, Anthropic's cheapest Opus in a generation is also the one it rates safest, even though its own tests may not catch everything.
Article Summary: Anthropic's new Claude Opus 5.5 is 40% cheaper than its predecessor. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessors. The model is available now on the Claude Platform.

Article Title: 1980s AI photo trend: Delhi Police warns users of fake profiles, blackmail and cyber fraud
Article Text:
1980s AI photo trend: Delhi Police warns users of fake profiles, blackmail and cyber fraud (Image Source: Delhi Police/Twitter)

Delhi Police warns against uploading photos on unknown AI tools

What is 1980s AI photo trend

The 1980s AI photo trend may look like harmless nostalgia, but Delhi Police has a warning for users. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Delhi Police asked users to be careful before uploading their photos to AI tools. The post stated that images uploaded online can be misused to create fake profiles, carry out fraud or blackmail people. “Looks like nostalgia but it could be a trap,” Delhi Police said in its post. “Your images can be misused for fake profiles, blackmail or cyber fraud,” it added.The warning comes as AI photo tools and filters allow users to transform modern pictures into images that look like they were taken decades ago. Delhi Police's post specifically used the “80s Photo Scam” theme to highlight the risks linked to sharing personal images online.Delhi Police urged users to think carefully before uploading their photos to unknown AI tools. The police warning says: “DON'T UPLOAD YOUR PHOTO: Unknown Al tools can misuse your images”. It further advises users to not click on random link as a “filter can hide a scam.“YOUR PHOTO YOUR IDENTITY,” the post warns adding that the uploaded photos can be misused and eventually “lead to fake profiles, fraud, blackmail or cybercrime”.The warning also directs people who face cyber fraud to report it through 1930, the cyber fraud helpline, or the government’s cybercrime reporting website.The police message comes with a simple warning for people taking part in the 1980s AI photo trend: enjoy the nostalgia, but be careful about where personal photos are uploaded and which links are opened.Popular among social media users, the 1980s AI photo trend uses AI to transform modern photos into images that look like they were taken in the 1980s. The images often feature vintage colours, old-style clothing, hairstyles and camera effects, giving people a retro look.
Article Summary: Delhi Police warns against uploading photos to unknown AI tools. The 1980s AI photo trend uses AI to transform modern photos into images that look like they were taken in the 1980s. Delhi Police says images can be misused to create fake profiles, carry out fraud or blackmail people.

Article Title: Apple is building a screenless Whoop rival, but it may not launch before 2028
Article Text:
Apple Watch is already copying Whoop and Oura, a band is the next step

Apple is developing a screenless fitness tracker to take on Whoop, the wearable maker now valued at around $10 billion. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple has spent several months exploring the category and is now building prototypes of a band that drops the display entirely.The early hardware pairs a thin fabric strap with a small computing module packed with sensors. Apple hasn't decided whether the product will ship. The project sits in an internal stage called a "technology investigation," and even if it moves ahead, a launch before 2028 looks unlikely. Apple declined to comment.The idea has backing from the top. Gurman reports that executive chairman Tim Cook and services chief Eddy Cue have taken a keen interest. Cue took over Apple's health teams late last year and has pushed them to borrow from newer rivals built around simpler interfaces. Engineers from Apple's Vision hardware group, the team behind Vision Pro, have also worked on the tracker.Markets noticed. Garmin, which sells display-free bands of its own, saw its shares fall as much as 2.5% after the report, while Apple stock rose about 1%.Apple remains one of the biggest smartwatch sellers, especially in the US.But Whoop and Oura have each built user bases in the millions by offering focused health tracking without apps or notifications. Oura filed for its IPO this month and is looking to raise up to $2.2 billion, while Whoop has said a listing is on the table. Google has entered the space too, with the Fitbit Air.Apple has already started borrowing from this crowd. The Apple Watch Series 12 and the revamped Health app bring a daily readiness score, more advanced heart rate tracking and an estimate of biological age. Whoop and Oura users will find all three familiar.The work also comes during a leadership change in Apple's health division. Former COO Jeff Williams retired at the end of last year, while Apple Watch marketing lead Stan Ng and fitness chief Jay Blahnik have both left.A screenless band would give Apple something it currently lacks: a way to sell its health tracking to people who don't want a smartwatch, including those unwilling to give up a mechanical watch. Before that, Apple is expected to launch smart glasses and camera-equipped AirPods in 2027, with a redesigned Apple Watch due as early as late 2027.
Article Summary: Apple is developing a screenless fitness tracker to take on Whoop and Oura. The company is building prototypes of a band that drops the display entirely. Early hardware pairs a thin fabric strap with a small computing module. The project sits in an internal stage called a "technology investigation"

Article Title: Boat launches smart earbuds range with Crest AI; offers Airdopes Prime 800 D, Airdopes Prime 701 ANC and Nirvana Ion ANC earbuds
Article Text:
Boat launches smart earbuds range with CREST AI

Boat has launched its first smart audio devices range featuring Boat Crest AI, its AI-powered platform built with Google Gemini. The lineup includes Boat Airdopes Prime 800, Boat Airdopes Prime 701 ANC and Boat Nirvana Ion ANC. With the launch, Boat is introducing a new proposition for personal audio — ‘Intelligent Ears’ — earbuds designed not just for listening, but to listen, understand, converse and assist.In a press release, the company said that the Crest AI is built around a simpler idea: bringing intelligence to something consumers already wear throughout their day — their earbuds. At the heart of the experience are three capabilities — Crest Ask, G- Assist and Crest Translate, or simply: Ask. Assist. Translate.With Crest Ask, users can ask questions, explore ideas, learn and have natural conversations with AI. Instead of repeatedly reaching for a phone or typing a query, users can ask follow-up questions and continue the conversation through their earbuds.With G- Assist take the experience from conversation to action. With integration across Google Gmail, Tasks, and Calendar, users can access everyday productivity and communication capabilities through voice.From asking the assistant to “summarize my day” to “reply to an email,” G-Assist helps users manage tasks, stay on top of schedules, and interact with their digital routines without reaching for their phones.Crest Translate enables real-time, two-way translation across 25+ languages, helping people speaking different languages communicate more naturally.Gaurav Nayyar, CEO, Boat said “Why should intelligence be limited to our rooms, desks, pockets or screens? We believe it can become much more natural and simply be with you. With Crest AI, built with Google Gemini, we are bringing that intelligence to your ears. Our idea of ‘Intelligent Ears’ is simple: earbuds that can listen, understand, converse and assist. But this is just the beginning, we are working on multiple other use cases. For ten years, Boat has helped India listen. Now, we want to help India listen, understand, converse and assist”.The Boat Airdopes Prime 800 D combines Crest AI capabilities with Dolby Audio and 11mm dynamic drivers tuned to Boat Signature Sound. The earbuds offer up to 45 hours of total playback, Multipoint Connectivity and four microphones with AI-ENx technology, bringing together entertainment, communication and intelligent assistance in one device.Crest AI is also available on the Boat Airdopes Prime 701 ANC and Boat Nirvana Ion ANC. The Boat Airdopes Prime 800 D, Boat Airdopes Prime 701 ANC and Boat Nirvana Ion ANC are available through the Boat website and leading e-commerce platforms.
Article Summary: Boat has launched its first smart audio devices range featuring Boat Crest AI, its AI-powered platform built with Google Gemini. At the heart of the experience are three capabilities — Crest Ask, G- Assist and Crest Translate. With the launch, Boat is introducing a new proposition for personal audio — 'Intelligent Ears'

Article Title: Motorola showcases Signature 27 with 50MP main camera and 200MP periscope telephoto camera
Article Text:
Motorola launches Signature 27 with 50MP main camera and 200MP periscope telephoto camera

Motorola Signature 27 features

Motorola Signature 27 operating system

Motorola has showcased the Signature 27, its second smartphone in the Signature series and one of the first phones announced with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The smartphone was unveiled at the Snapdragon Summit 2026 on Tuesday and comes with a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main camera and a 200MP periscope telephoto camera. Motorola is also changing its naming system with this phone, using the final two digits of the upcoming year for its new generations. The company has not yet announced the price or exact sale date, but says the Signature 27 will launch globally later this year.The Motorola Signature 27 is powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor. Motorola says the chipset brings improvements to on-device AI, camera performance, gaming response and download speeds. The phone also comes with Motorola’s ArcticMesh cooling system. It combines diamond-infused thermal gel, liquid metal and copper mesh with a redesigned 3D vapour chamber. Motorola says the new vapour chamber is 40% larger than the previous generation.Motorola Signature 27 gets a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main camera along with a 200MP periscope telephoto camera.Motorola has also introduced its Video Enhancement Engine, which uses AI to study a scene before and during video recording and adjust colour tones in real time.The phone will also support Google's Gemini Omni, which can use prompts, photos or existing video clips to create a finished video. Google's Lyria can be used to generate music and soundtracks.The phone will be available in Pantone Coal Smoke and Pantone Capulet Green. The Coal Smoke version has a woven texture designed to improve grip and durability, while Capulet Green gets a brushed, textile-inspired finish.Motorola says the Signature 27 will receive seven years of OS upgrades and is expected to launch with Android 17. It is also the company's first smartphone with Audio by B&O, with the branding etched onto the rear panel.Motorola has not yet revealed the phone's display, battery capacity, charging speed, RAM, storage or other camera sensors. Pricing and the exact launch date are also yet to be announced.
Article Summary: Motorola Signature 27 gets a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main camera along with a 200MP periscope telephoto camera. The phone is powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor. Motorola has not yet revealed the phone's display, battery capacity, charging speed, RAM, storage or other camera sensors.

Article Title: Portronics launches Mopcop Duo, a 3-in-1 cordless cleaning device
Article Text: Portronics has expanded its product portfolio in India with the launch of Mopcop Duo, a 3-in-1 cordless cleaning device designed to make everyday cleaning more convenient and efficient. MopCop Duo combines a vacuum cleaner, air blower, and floor mop in one compact device, offering a practical cleaning solution for homes and on-the-go use.The Mopcop Duo features a sleek white finish and a compact, lightweight design that makes it easy to carry, operate, and store. Its ergonomic build lets users move seamlessly between different cleaning needs, making it suitable for everyday household use and quick clean-ups on the go.Portronics Mopcop Duo is powered by a high-performance brushless motor that delivers up to 17,000Pa of suction, helping remove dust, crumbs, pet hair, and other everyday debris. The device offers two cleaning speed modes, indicated by Tiffany Blue and White LED lights, allowing users to select the appropriate level of cleaning performance. It runs on three 2000mAh rechargeable batteries, delivering up to 30 minutes of runtime for convenient cordless cleaning.Beyond vacuuming, the Mopcop Duo is equipped with air-blowing and floor-mopping capabilities, extending its utility across different cleaning tasks. The detachable 90° flexible mop rod provides added flexibility while cleaning and mopping floors. The blower is equipped with wide-to-narrow nozzles to accommodate different air-blowing requirements. Users can easily switch between the different modes depending on the surface or task at hand.For improved dust capture and easy maintenance, the device comes with a dual-layer washable HEPA filter designed to capture fine dust particles. A 90ml dust cup helps collect everyday debris, while a range of attachments enhances its usability across different spaces. These include a narrow vacuum nozzle for corners and tight spaces and an extended hose that provides additional reach for hard-to-access areas. The Mopcop Duo can be used across surfaces and spaces including floors, sofas, cars, computers, and other difficult-to-reach areas.Mopcop Duo supports Type-C charging, making it easy to recharge using compatible charging sources.Portronics Mopcop Duo has an MRP of Rs 6,999 and is currently listed at Rs 4,099 on Portronics.com. The product comes with a 1-year warranty and can also be purchased from Amazon.in, Flipkart.com, and other leading online and offline retail stores across India.
Article Summary: Portronics Mopcop Duo combines a vacuum cleaner, air blower, and floor mop in one compact device. It is powered by a high-performance brushless motor that delivers up to 17,000Pa of suction, helping remove dust, crumbs, pet hair, and other everyday debris. The device offers two cleaning speed modes, indicated by Tiffany Blue and White LED lights.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Students get hands-on training in CNC technology at AISSMS
Article Text:
Students get hands-on training in CNC technology at AISSMS

Pune:





Students of AISSMS Institute of Information Technology (AISSMS IOIT) received hands-on training in computer numerical control (CNC) technology during an internship programme conducted by the institute’s AICTE IDEA Lab.The programme covered CNC machine programming, operation and machining, along with advanced manufacturing processes. Students worked on actual machines as part of the programme, giving them practical experience in manufacturing processes and technical skills used in industry.The programme was conducted under the guidance of AISSMS IOIT principal Dr P B Mane and head of department Dr M Gajare. Dr Y P Patil, Dr M B Nigade and Devendra Itole coordinated the programme.The initiative was undertaken by the institute’s AICTE IDEA Lab to provide students with practical exposure to modern manufacturing technologies. The programme was organised under the guidance of secretary Malojiraje Chhatrapati.
Article Summary: Students of AISSMS Institute of Information Technology (AISSMS IOIT) received hands-on training in computer numerical control (CNC) technology. The training included exposure to CAD/CAM, CNC programming, digital manufacturing and other advanced manufacturing technologies.

Article Title: In 2005, a California engineer used Google Earth to challenge a logging plan above Los Gatos Creek; community pressure later helped spare 1,000 acres of redwood watershed
Article Text:
Rebecca Moore used 3D satellite mapping to visualise a proposed logging area in the Los Gatos Creek watershed near Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve, helping local residents understand the scale and location of the project. Credits - Wikipedia, science.nasa.gov

Making sense of the map

The evidence offered

Rebecca Moore, Google Earth Outreach leader, speaks alongside Chief Almir of the Paiter-Surui people and members of the Surui community at a 2012 press conference in Rio de Janeiro, where Google launched the Surui Cultural Map. Credits - science.nasa.gov

A campaign that made a difference

Residents who oppose corporate development plans frequently find it difficult to understand complicated legal notifications and technical maps that unexpectedly arrive in the mail. When a group of landowners in the Santa Cruz Mountains of California got an official notification in 2005 detailing a proposal to chop a sizable area of forest above their homes, they found themselves in precisely that predicament. What transpired became one of the first instances of ordinary people using digital mapping technology to oppose a powerful organisation and alter the course of a local environmental battle.The warning was from the San Jose Water Company, a company that owns about 6,000 acres in the Los Gatos Creek watershed, a source of drinking water for more than 100,000 people in Silicon Valley. The company submitted a plan in August 2005 to cut about 1,000 acres of forest including coast redwoods and Douglas fir along a six-mile section of canyon, and copies of a black and white map explaining the plan were mailed to neighbouring people.For many, the document was almost impossible to comprehend as it gave little differentiation between roads, contour lines and the real borders of the proposed logging zone.One of the residents to get the warning was engineer Rebecca Moore, who was working on a mapping tool within Google that would become known as Google Earth Outreach . Instead of relying on the confused paper map, Moore set out to make her own map using satellite imagery and aerial pictures of the entire watershed. She helped create a neighbourhood group, Neighbours Against Irresponsible Logging, and utilised the new Google Earth software to map the proposed logging area much more accurately than the utility’s initial document had done.Moore’s computer map did more than map out boundaries. She layered in geo-located photographs of old-growth redwoods that stood in the way of the plan, added sightings of local wildlife such as ospreys and beavers, and imported data that showed that endangered red-legged frogs lived in the canyon, directly contradicting the company’s claim that no protected species were present. She also teamed with a colleague to build a three-dimensional flypast of a simulated helicopter carrying cut redwood trunks on a flight path over nearby schools and residences.Moore’s presentation of her flypast at the group’s inaugural community gathering had an instant impact. Residents who had failed to interpret a flat printed map could suddenly see, in three dimensions, how narrow mountain roads laced with more than 30 blind curves would convey a dozen 90,000-pound logging trucks each day past pathways frequented by children heading to school. The presentation gave the community a common and correct picture of exactly what the logging plan would do for their neighbourhood, which the initial notification had not provided.Separately, opponents of the plan objected to the size of the company’s assets. Residents said their own aerial surveys showed the company’s actual holdings exceeded a ceiling set by California law on the amount of commercially harvestable forest a single owner could hold and still qualify for the kind of open-ended logging permit the water company wanted. The issue was sent to California’s forestry regulator, which has standards for assessing proposals like these established by the CAL FIRE Board of Forestry and Fire Protection.Eventually community pressure and more regulatory issues pushed a turning point. By December 2007, almost two years after the original notice was mailed, the water company had withdrawn its logging proposal, and California’s forestry department had found the plan invalid under the laws that governed it. The result, for the redwood watershed above Los Gatos, was that some 1,000 acres of forest were saved from the large-scale cutting which the original plan had called for.The episode also had repercussions well beyond a small canyon in California. Moore’s success in using Google Earth to expose the difference between a company’s official map and the actual size of its plans became one of the origin stories for Google Earth Outreach, a programme designed specifically to help environmental and community groups use mapping technology in their own campaigns. Moore has said the fight above Los Gatos Creek influenced her later work creating tools to detect deforestation and environmental change across continents.Today, San Jose Water owns and manages thousands of acres in the same watershed and describes its approach to the property in terms of long-term stewardship rather than massive-scale timber harvesting. The 2005 controversy is one of the most startling early examples of how accessible digital mapping can shift the power from major institutions to locals, changing what may have been an intractable bureaucratic war into a contest that ordinary people could see clearly enough to win.
Article Summary: Rebecca Moore used 3D satellite mapping to visualise a proposed logging area in the Los Gatos Creek watershed near Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve. She helped create a neighbourhood group, Neighbours Against Irresponsible Logging, and utilised the new Google Earth software to map the proposed area.

Article Title: Pennsylvania's youth business fair grew from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026; kids ages 5 to 16 handled their own products, pricing and sales with no adults behind the tables
Article Text:
Representative image from Canva

A kitchen-table idea becomes a regional tradition

The rule that makes it real: no adults behind the table

How kids prepare their businesses

A marketplace of ideas and products

Judges, awards and encouragement

Part of a larger movement

Why this matters for families and schools

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Kidpreneurs Fair do you think benefits kids the most? Learning to manage money Gaining customer service skills Enhancing creativity 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pennsylvania's youth business fair has grown from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026, turning a small community gathering into one of Central PA's most visible celebrations of kid-led enterprise. Children aged 5 to 16 run their own stalls, handling products, pricing, marketing and sales with no adults behind the tables, while parents and volunteers stay in the background as shoppers and supporters. The event, known as the Kidpreneurs Fair PA and hosted in Mechanicsburg, is part of the wider Acton Children's Business Fair network and is organised by local parents Ashruta Shettar and Pradeep Patil, who say the goal is to let kids learn entrepreneurship by doing rather than by watching, according to the fair's official site and the Children's Business Fair listing.The Kidpreneurs Fair PA began around a family kitchen table in 2022. Ashruta Shettar and Pradeep Patil, IT professionals and small-business owners, were watching their twin daughters dream up products and realised that their children would learn more by actually selling something than by talking about business in the abstract. They set up the first fair with 60 young entrepreneurs, offering each child a simple booth, a table and a chance to test their ideas with real customers.From that first event, the fair quickly became a local tradition. In 2024, participation grew to more than 85 kidpreneurs, with families turning out in large numbers to support everything from handmade crafts to original recipes. By 2025, nearly 160 children filled the marketplace, and some participants began converting their fair-day experiments into ongoing micro-businesses that operated beyond the single event. The 2026 edition capped booths at 100 and added a special touch, with personalised letters from the Governor of Pennsylvania for every participant, signalling how far the fair had come in just a few years.The most distinctive feature of the fair is its core rule. Parents may help with the application and with transport, but on fair day, children must run their own booths. They set up their displays, greet customers, explain their products, handle money and make change. Adults are welcome as shoppers and cheerleaders, but they are not allowed to sell or promote a child's product. If a parent is found doing so, the child's business can be disqualified from the competition.This rule is designed to give children an authentic experience of entrepreneurship. It means that a 6-year-old selling friendship bracelets must decide how much to charge, how to arrange the table and how to talk to strangers about their work. A 14-year-old offering custom keychains or baked goods must think about costs, profit margins and how to stand out in a busy marketplace. The fair becomes a safe space to make mistakes, learn from them and try again next year with a better plan.The application process itself is part of the learning. Children are asked to describe their product or service, set a price, estimate costs and explain how they will cover startup expenses. They must outline how they will advertise before the fair and how they will judge success at the end. Parents can assist with writing and calculations, but the expectation is that children do as much as possible on their own, appropriate to their age.Businesses are judged in six age categories, from 5 to 6 years old up to 15 to 16. Mixed-age groups are judged in the category of the oldest participant, and up to three children can share a single booth. The application fee is $35 per booth, fully refundable if the business is not accepted or if the family cancels at least a week before the event. Accepted applicants are notified on a rolling basis until the 100-booth cap is reached, creating a sense of urgency and planning for young founders.Walking through the fair feels like visiting a miniature version of a farmers market or craft fair, except every vendor is under 17. Booths feature handmade jewellery, slime and sensory toys, custom T-shirts, baked goods, art prints, pet treats, bath bombs and small services such as lawn care or tech help for neighbours. Some children build on hobbies, turning a love of drawing or baking into a branded product line. Others experiment with entirely new ideas, testing whether there is demand for a concept they have never tried before.Each business is given an 8-foot table, shared with one other vendor, under a tented outdoor setup at Messiah University's Eisenhower Campus Center in Mechanicsburg. Tablecloths are not provided, and electricity is not available, so children must design displays that work with simple materials. This constraint encourages creativity. A well-arranged table with clear pricing, attractive samples and a friendly pitch can make a big difference in how many customers stop and buy.A panel of local business leaders, educators and community figures serves as judges for the fair. Past and current judges have included school heads, CEOs of regional organisations, commissioners from state advisory bodies, owners of small businesses and representatives from major employers such as The Hershey Company and IKEA. They evaluate each business on creativity, presentation and entrepreneurial spirit, offering feedback that is meant to encourage young founders long after the fair ends.While prizes and recognition matter, the organisers stress that the real reward is the experience. Children leave with a clearer sense of what it takes to run a business, from costing and pricing to customer service and marketing. Some go on to expand their fair-day ventures into regular income streams, selling online or at local markets. Others simply gain confidence, realising that they can create something, put it in front of strangers and handle the entire transaction themselves.The Kidpreneurs Fair PA is part of the Acton Children's Business Fair network, which began in Austin, Texas, in 2007. That first event had just seven young entrepreneurs and about 25 attendees. Today, the Austin fair hosts more than 115 kidpreneurs and draws around 1,500 visitors, and similar fairs run in cities and towns across North America. The model is intentionally simple and replicable, relying on local hosts, volunteers and small sponsors to bring the experience to their own communities.In Pennsylvania, the fair is proudly sponsored by Sugaring NYC and supported by local donors and volunteers. The organisers say they believe principled entrepreneurs are heroes and role models for the next generation, whether they become famous business leaders or remain unsung owners of small neighbourhood enterprises. By giving children a structured, supportive environment to try entrepreneurship early, they hope to nurture a generation that sees business as a way to solve problems, serve others and build independence.For parents and educators, the fair offers a practical complement to classroom learning. Children apply maths when they calculate costs and profits, use language arts when they write product descriptions and signage, and practise social skills when they interact with customers. They also learn resilience. Not every product sells out, not every display attracts a crowd, and not every idea works the first time. Those lessons, experienced in a low-stakes setting, can shape how children approach challenges in school and later in work.As the Kidpreneurs Fair PA continues to grow, its organisers face choices about how big to go, how to maintain quality and how to keep the focus on learning rather than competition. For now, the trajectory from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026 suggests strong demand from families who want their children to have this kind of hands-on experience. In a region known for its small businesses and community spirit, the fair has become a place where the next generation can practise being founders, one table at a time.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania's youth business fair has grown from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026. Children aged 5 to 16 run their own stalls, handling products, pricing, marketing and sales with no adults behind the tables. Adults are welcome as shoppers and cheerleaders, but they are not allowed to sell or promote a child's product.

Article Title: In 2013, Canadian teenager Ann Makosinski invented a flashlight powered by body heat; now she is creating colourful toys to teach children about renewable energy
Article Text:
A new kind of light

eDrink : A mug that generates electricity

Toys with renewable energy

They say some children are born prodigies, and when it comes to Ann Makosinski, the statement holds true. As a teenager living in Canada, her friend living in the Philippines told her that she couldn't study at night since her family couldn't afford electricity to turn the lights on. Soon she wondered if there was a way to have light without traditional electricity. This is when she came up with a record-making invention, a flashlight powered by body heat.Like other children her age, Makosinski did not watch television or play video games. She spent her time listening to the opera, watching silent movies and learning to play the piano and violin. Interestingly, her first toy was a box of transistors. “I wasn’t given many toys, so I had to make my own,” she said to CNN back in 2019. “I would take garbage and my hot glue gun from around the house and piece together these so-called inventions, and obviously they never worked, but the idea of taking things from around me and piecing them together to make something better just kind of came really naturally. ”Makosinski was only 15 when she invented a flashlight that was powered by the heat of the user's hands.The Hollow Flashlight uses thermoelectric technology to convert the temperature difference between the user's hand and the surrounding air into electricity. The device uses Peltier tiles, which generate electricity when one side is heated by the palm of the hand and the other is cooled.No batteries are required, with the flashlight running entirely on human body heat that would otherwise go to waste. School students, therefore, could study without worrying about running out of battery power.The Hollow Flashlight earned Makosinski a win in the 15-16 age category at the 2013 Google Science Fair and won at the 2014 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair. Her wins made her an international media sensation. She made appearances on shows such as 'The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon' and was featured in publications such as TIME and Forbes. She even gave a TEDxTeen Talk titled 'Why I don't use a smartphone'. Makosinski only bought her first phone, an old-fashioned flip model, at the age of 18.The intrigued teenager did not stop there. Soon, she launched her next major invention, the eDrink. At 18, while enrolled at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, she designed a coffee mug to capture the excess heat from a hot beverage and convert it into electricity. This excess energy could then be used to provide a small charge to a phone or other device for 30 minutes. It uses Peltier tiles (thermoelectric generators), and by heating one side of the tiles with your drink and cooling the other side with the design of the mug (and a bunch of electronic circuits, of course), electricity is produced."I got the inspiration for my project when I noticed that my high school friends were always complaining about their phones dying too soon and that their coffee was too hot to drink," she told Society for Science.Now 29, Makosinski is looking to inspire other young girls across the world to use their minds and creativity in a similar fashion. Her interest in thermoelectric technology has led her toward a different kind of invention: toys designed to teach children about renewable energy.She has created bright-coloured toys that help kids learn about renewable energy in exciting ways. They can see and play with it as it lights up, spins or makes sound when powered by sunlight, water or a hand-wound mechanism.The goal now, she told CNN, is to have other youngsters, girls in particular, follow her into the world of science.“I just want, especially young kids, to feel like they can invent their own solutions and they don’t have to wait for other people to make them,” said Makosinski, who described herself as “a normal girl who just used her time differently after school.”“I want to inspire people to be more creative with the resources they have around them,” she added.
Article Summary: Ann Makosinski was 15 when she invented a flashlight powered by body heat. At 18, she designed a coffee mug to capture excess heat from a hot beverage and convert it into electricity. Now 29, she is looking to inspire other young girls across the world to use their minds and creativity.

Article Title: Meet Shriyan Avadhanula, the 16-year-old Virginia student who built a free college-prep platform after getting frustrated by paid resources; Scholark has crossed 10,000 users
Article Text: College applications involve more than just writing essays; they also demand that students scour through a thousand websites in need of information, process it on their own and spend an enormous amount of time, doing everything rather than applying. Frustrated with the scattered, costly resources for college preparation, a 16-year-old high school student in Virginia saw an opportunity to help others like him out.Shriyan Avadhanula was juggling his IB coursework, varsity soccer, and competitive pickleball while also being a junior at Henrico High School in Virginia. At the same time, he was navigating college websites, GPA calculators, SAT resources and test preparation platforms. According to him, the information he wanted usually existed, but it was scattered across different websites, sometimes difficult to interpret and often behind paywalls.“I used to have a bunch of tabs up on my computer, where it's like a GPA calculator, college websites, SAT resources — all of that stuff was so overwhelming,” he said.Eventually, during his freshman year, he decided to see if he could build a better alternative himself.What he began as a basic GPA calculator and college admissions prediction tool, eventually became Scholark, a free digital platform that now includes AP test preparation and college admissions resources. Avadhanula estimated he spent roughly two and a half to three years building and revising it, adding features as he encountered new needs as a student himself.It wasn't that information was not available about college; but Avadhanula said that it was presented in a disjointed way and still students like him were trying to use it. “Why not just build a platform ... I can use with everyone else?” he recalled thinking.College websites can present students with statistics, admissions requirements and other information within what Avadhanula described as a “big wall of text.” With Scholark — which Avadhanula noted ends with a ‘K’ for visually aesthetic purposes- he sought to organise information around the questions and resources he and other students were looking for.Another consideration was the cost. While preparing for his AP Computer Science Principles exam, Avadhanula recalled completing roughly 50 practice questions through an online resource before encountering a prompt asking him to pay $49.99 for a subscription to see his score. “That really, really annoyed me and frustrated me,” he said. “And I realised that wasn't the only place that does it.” Moreover, he said that experience reinforced his desire to keep Scholark free.The platform’s earliest iteration was much simpler than it is today, with a GPA calculator and an AP study guide component he initially built to help himself prepare for AP Computer Science Principles with better practice materials. Learning some of the technical skills needed to build it through online programs and from his father, who works in software development, Avadhanula said he built Scholark using website tools like HTML, CSS and, primarily, JavaScript. As the project progressed, he also began using artificial intelligence to help identify bugs in thousands of lines of code.“I remember spending countless nights, no sleep, just trying to learn how [the College Board] make their questions," he said. “And then I learned. I made, I think, 50 questions on how they phrase it, and then trained my AI agent to continue making questions like that the way I did it, and that's where it started making them more accurate.” The process paid off for him personally, Avadhanula said he used the early version of the platform to study for the aforementioned AP Computer Science Principles exam and earned a four out of five.From there, Avadhanula said Scholark kept growing, adding more college-planning resources, including an admissions prediction feature that compares information students enter with publicly available admissions data.That feature grew out of another problem he encountered as a user, different admissions websites could give substantially different predictions, without always making it clear where those estimates came from. Scholark shows users the data behind its estimates, he said, though he is careful not to present the results as definitive. “I'm not going to claim that it's 100 per cent accurate because I don't believe anything is 100 per cent accurate, because there's always room to grow,” he said.Avadhanula shared Scholark with friends, asked them to be candid about what worked and what didn't, and continued making changes based on their feedback. But then people he didn't know started finding and using it. Avadhanula said more than 10,000 users have accessed Scholark since its launch in 2025, with traffic peaking around AP exam season as students searched for free study resources. Seeing that growth was unexpected, he said, particularly for something that began as a tool he had built for himself. “I didn't think people would actually use it,” he said.Now, those users give him another reason to keep tinkering with a platform he still considers a work in progress, but the perspective that prompted him to start building it hasn't changed: He is still one of the students trying to navigate the information Scholark was designed to curate.“I made the whole UI [user interface] itself very easy to access, very student-like, because I'm a student as well,” Avadhanula said. “I know what a student wants to see.”
Article Summary: Shriyan Avadhanula, a 16-year-old high school student in Virginia, built Scholark, a free digital platform that now includes AP test preparation and college admissions resources. He spent roughly two and a half to three years building and revising it, adding features as he encountered new needs as a student.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape
Article Text:
From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape

Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.

From discarded tyres to footwear with a purpose, the idea began with a childhood experience. At the age of 10, UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar visited rural Africa, where he saw children walking long distances barefoot, often without adequate footwear.Moved by what he witnessed, Ahaan gave away his favourite pair of slippers to a child he met during the visit. The experience stayed with him long after he returned home and eventually became the starting point for a larger idea.As he grew older, Ahaan began exploring how discarded materials could be repurposed to address the lack of affordable, durable footwear. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles.The idea brought together two concerns he had encountered separately: the growing problem of tyre waste and the need for accessible footwear.He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala, and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day. Ahaan then connected with Mamco General Trading, which operates in Uganda and Zambia. As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility programme, the company will purchase 4,000 pairs of slippers each month for free distribution to children and families in need. It’s a sustainable cycle that turns waste into opportunity, supporting livelihoods and giving kids durable footwear.“When I was 10 years old, I saw children my age walking barefoot, and I never forgot that moment,” Ahaan says. “I wanted to create something that could help people and the environment. If we can turn discarded tyres into something useful and long-lasting, maybe it can inspire more young people to believe their simple ideas can really make a difference.”The world’s growing dependence on convenience and mobility comes with an environmental cost. Every year, more than a billion tyres reach the end of their usable life, creating a significant waste-management challenge. Many of these tyres end up in landfills, while others are burned or processed in ways that can contribute to pollution and the loss of valuable materials.Repurposing discarded tyres offers one way to address this challenge by keeping materials in use for longer and reducing the amount of waste that needs to be disposed of. Turning old tyres into durable slipper soles, for instance, gives a material that would otherwise be discarded a new application while also reducing the need for virgin raw materials in footwear production.The approach reflects a broader shift in how sustainability is being understood. Rather than treating waste simply as something to be collected and discarded, initiatives like this explore how materials already in circulation can be redesigned and put to practical use.In doing so, they can support waste reduction, resource conservation and efforts to lower the environmental impact associated with new production. Ultimately, sustainability is not only about recycling what has already been used, but also about rethinking waste as a potential resource.
Article Summary: UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar saw children walking barefoot in rural Africa. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles. He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day.

Article Title: AI malware is becoming its own category: Researchers found a malicious program that uses multiple AI models to decide what to do
Article Text:
AI malware is becoming its own category: Researchers found a malicious program that uses multiple AI models to decide what to do

How does the AI-powered malware work

Researchers are finding more AI-powered malware

What the findings suggest

Researchers have reportedly found a malicious program that uses AI model to help decide what it should do next. The malware, called CLOSEDQUORUM, can contact up to four AI models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini. Instead of relying only on instructions written by its developers, the program asks these AI systems for guidance and uses their responses to decide its next steps. Reported by Wired, the discovery was made by researchers at Cisco Talos, who have also created an open-source framework to track malware that uses AI.CLOSEDQUORUM is designed for Windows and can use several AI services at the same time. Researchers describe the setup as a kind of “hive mind”, because the malware can seek decisions from multiple AI models. If one AI service is unavailable, the others can continue working.As stated in the report, researchers also found no mechanism that would allow a human to step in and control the process.The malware is designed to steal login credentials and cryptocurrency. Researchers also found links to cybercrime forums discussing credit-card fraud dating back to 2025. However, they could not confirm who created CLOSEDQUORUM or whether it has been used in real-world attacks.Cisco Talos created the Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network (CAIRN) after researchers began finding signs that attackers were integrating AI into malware.Ryan Fetterman of Cisco Talos said AI integration leaves behind identifiable “fingerprints” that can help researchers track and classify these programs.“The core idea is that AI integration has these vestiges, like fingerprints, that are left behind... That gives us a signal that we can use to track these samples, classify them, and look at what's happening,” Fetterman said.When Fetterman first searched for AI-integrated malware, he found only around nine named malware families, along with several proof-of-concept examples. After CAIRN was developed, researchers identified about 20 additional examples within a few months.The findings suggest that AI is becoming more deeply integrated into some malware rather than simply being used by hackers to write code or create phishing messages. Matt Olney of Cisco Talos said attackers are now beginning to operationalise AI.“Initially, everyone saw AI as a productivity tool, right?... Now what we're seeing is that it's becoming operationalized.”He said AI could allow attackers to run more campaigns, target more systems and handle different computers because the technology can provide responses and guidance in the background.
Article Summary: Malware can contact up to four AI models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini. Researchers describe setup as a kind of ‘hive mind’ because the malware can seek decisions from multiple AI models. If one AI service is unavailable, the others can continue working.

Article Title: Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle with EvenHeat technology
Article Text:
Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle price and availability

Nuuk has launched SĒRV MAX, claiming it to be India’s first 100% food-safe multi-cook kettle featuring its EvenHeat engineered coil. Designed and made in India, SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element to distribute heat more evenly. It is paired with SĒRV WARM Mode which maintains cooked food at a steady 65°C until it is ready to be served. The appliance features 1.3L capacity, 2+1 cooking modes, and a SteelTech SUS304 stainless-steel interior, while the SteamTray included in the launch bundle adds another layer of functionality to it.The Nuuk SĒRV MAX is available at a launch price of Rs 2,699, with the SteamTray included, in Nuuk Red and Serene Grey colours. It is available on Nuuk website (Amazon, Blinkit and offline availability to go live by October).The product is made in India through Nuuk’s India-based manufacturing partnerships, reflecting the brand’s approach to building appliances around the realities of Indian homes. From chai and Maggi to idlis, dal and quick meals between busy schedules, it has been developed with food habits and everyday kitchen routines in mind.With its extra-large capacity, SĒRV MAX is built to accommodate approximately five cups at a time, offering more room for everyday preparations beyond a single cup of tea or coffee. Its two heat levels, alongside SĒRV WARM, allow it to adapt across different cooking needs, from boiled eggs and breakfast preparations to noodles, soup and rice.The SteamTray, with a 200 cm² steaming area, adds another layer of versatility, allowing users to steam momos, dumplings and vegetables.The product features SteelTech, a SUS304 stainless-steel interior that is food-grade, rust-proof and designed for everyday cooking without a conventional non-stick coating. This provides a durable cooking surface without relying on coatings that can scratch or flake with use.The appliance also features 5-Layer Ultimate SafetyTech, combining auto cut-off, boil-dry protection, overheat protection and thermal fuse protection. Its SafeTouch cool-touch body is designed to remain comfortable to hold even while the contents are boiling inside.“We believe that familiar appliances deserve to evolve with the way we live today. The kettle has long been a convenient part of Indian kitchens, but there is an opportunity to make it far more useful without making it more complicated. With SĒRV MAX, we set out to rethink this everyday format through more consistent heating, the flexibility to cook and keep food warm, a larger capacity, and a food-safe stainless-steel interior, rust-free, leach-free and heat-stable for daily boing and cooking. The kettle has been designed with real Indian cooking routines in mind, from the EvenHeat technology to the SĒRV WARM Mode. Our goal is to make everyday cooking more convenient,considered and safe, while staying true to our belief that thoughtful design should always serve a real consumer need,” said Gazal Kalra, Co-Founder, Nuuk.
Article Summary: SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element. Article Title: Palo Alto Networks taps Anthropic and OpenAI to automate corporate cyber defence
Article Text:
Always-on offensive testing and attack path mapping

Palo Alto Networks has announced an enterprise-grade cybersecurity service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) models from Anthropic and OpenAI , aiming to identify and neutralise network vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them. The deployment comes as cybercriminals increasingly rely on automated algorithms to locate and breach enterprise weaknesses, prompting security companies to build counter-defenses capable of matching automated hacking cycles. Dubbed Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, the platform pairs open-weight architectures with cybersecurity-tailored systems, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Cyber.Unlike traditional periodic vulnerability scans, the service operates as an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. According to the company, the system continuously evaluates web applications, application programming interfaces (APIs), and cloud infrastructure. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors.“Threat actors today are deploying AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities, compressing breach cycles by almost 97% in some cases, from weeks to hours. To help defenders answer the critical question of whether they are prepared for this step-change in cybersecurity, Unit 42 is now offering continuous offensive testing to identify and validate vulnerabilities, pinpoint exposures and attack paths, and then accelerate remediation,” the company said.Beyond locating security gaps, Palo Alto Networks stated that the service delivers actionable mitigation guidance. This includes step-by-step code repairs alongside virtual patching solutions to shield assets before a permanent fix is integrated.“Palo Alto Networks developed and validated this approach over six months of in-house testing and across more than 100 Unit 42 customer engagements, backed by a $17 million investment in R&D and methodology optimization. During internal deployment within Palo Alto Networks, the company found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks. In customer assessments, the Frontier AI Exposure Analysis found exposures in 100% of customers. Of those, 37% rated high or critical in severity. Overall, most exposures stemmed from first-party apps and more than two in three exposures in third-party apps had no known CVE,” the company added.The company confirmed that the tool will be available internationally on an annual subscription basis. Pricing tiers will depend directly on the specific combination of OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-source models chosen by each enterprise client.
Article Summary: Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense is an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors. Palo Alto Networks found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks.
